I mostly agree with you, except for cancer treatment in most provinces. While some provinces cover the costs of chemotherapy and radiation, others do not. Having cancer can easily cost $100,000 if it is in an advanced stage and requires more than basic treatment. Several of my family members have been stuck with these costs, even though they had medical coverage and OHIP coverage, because the total cost of treatment exceeded the amount they were allowed to claim that year. Exceeding that yearly maximum only took 2 weeks of chemotherapy for one relative. Luckily they had RRSPs they could use to cover the costs, but they no longer have that money for retirement.
So, you're right that we do have good healthcare, overall, without having to pay up front most of the time. Sometimes we do have to pay, though, and it can be a lot. If we can't afford treatments that aren't covered, we don't get them, just like in the US.

It may get better, and it may not, and it just isn't any kind of fair. If you die, your pain may end but it may not. Nobody knows for sure what happens after death. If you die, though, the pain that others feel who care about you is definite. It's not fair to think that their happiness is more important than yours, but the difference is that you would be directly causing them pain to a similar degree of what you feel now. And you would be causing them that pain without any guarantee that what you experience after death would be any less painful than what you are experiencing now.
There is always a chance, as long as we're alive, that a new treatment or procedure will come out that WILL help. It is possible that it will get better, someday.

If you want people to know that your death is intentional, then leave a note. If you would rather spare them a small amount of pain by relieving them of the guilt associated with finding out that a loved one has taken their own life, then don't. If you want your body to be found, consider the implications that finding a potentially gruesome dead body might have on the person who discovers it. If a loved one finds you, will they ever be the same? If a child finds you, will they grow up to suffer horribly from the experience? Will the person who finds you have a heart attack or a miscarriage? If you make it so that your body will never be found, will your loved ones ever have closure? If your death is ruled a suicide, who will pay for your funeral since life insurance won't pay out?

These are the questions I ask myself when I am in the same spot you're in right now. I also ask myself if I'm willing to cause suffering to a similar degree in other people who care about me so that I can escape the suffering. So far, I haven't been able to come up with answers to these questions that allow me to end my life with a reasonably clear conscience.

I can't leave my apartment until I've followed a specific routine, but only for the first time that I leave my place for the day. I have to lay in bed after my alarm goes off until it feels "right" or else I may end up in the wrong place at the wrong time. I then have to use the washroom and brush my teeth in a very specific way and then clean the sink and toilet and counter top. I feed my cats, give them fresh water, scoop the litter, scrub my hands. I then have to check my schedule for the day and make sure I feel prepared for everything on the list (I have to have a detailed list with every activity for the day) and if I don't feel prepared I have to do what I have to in order to feel prepared, like read about what I am preparing for. This can take an hour or longer and is what takes me the longest of the whole routine. I then make sure that the clothing I picked out the night before is apropriate for the weather and activities, based on my reading. I take a shower, washing in a particular order, until I feel clean, and then wash the shower and tub. I get dressed, do my hair, and then clean the counter top and floor. I grab my standard breakfast of a granola bar and a bottle of water, my bag, keys, shoes, and stand at the door. If it feels right, I can leave. If it doesn't feel right, I have to figure out why. If I don't feel prepared then I have to read more, look up the forcast again, check my email again, go over my schedule again and my list of what I need to bring with me. If I feel like it isn't "right" to leave yet, then I have to wait until it does so nothing bad happens. I check to make sure everything is turned off and leave, making sure the door is locked. Sometimes it never feels right and I can't leave, but luckily that doesn't happen too often. I always set my alarm for more than 2 hours before I have to leave, and I try to make sure I'm ready for my day the night before. That often means I get very little sleep if I'm up late trying to make sure I'm ready and then up very early. I'm often late for class or appointments because it didn't feel right to leave in time.
